    Are You a Scientist?

    Rankings are everywhere in academia. The numbers keep going up and mean less every year — it is time we talked about what we built universities for.

    By Ronaldo Menezes
    Written in Exeter, United Kingdom

    Are you a scientist? If you are, you are constantly flooded by rankings. There are rankings everywhere, for everything you can imagine. They usually fall into the two areas that make up the core of academic life, research and teaching, but over the years they have multiplied in a way I have rarely seen anywhere else. What are they for? Why do we care so much about them? In this post I will argue that some form of ranking may be necessary, but that rankings as they exist today often do more harm than good, because they pull our attention towards the metric and away from the purpose of what we do as scientists. I am describing the general picture across universities, not any particular institution. There are always exceptions, and the views here are entirely my own.

    The corporate world offers an interesting contrast. Companies are measured too, of course, but they seem far less consumed by rankings than we are, and I suspect the reason is that their purpose is clear. A company exists to make a profit, and profit tells it, quite directly, whether it is succeeding. Academia has a purpose that is just as clear, if we choose to hold on to it: to educate people and to generate knowledge. The difficulty is that this purpose is much harder to measure, so we built layer upon layer of metrics to evaluate ourselves, and over time we started living by them. Perhaps we should take a lesson from the corporate world here. If we kept our attention on educating and generating knowledge, and did that well, the rankings would follow as a consequence, instead of sitting at the centre of everything we do.

    On the research side, which is the focus of this post, there was a time when two numbers did most of the work: how many papers you had published and how many times they had been cited. Back then, counting publications made a certain amount of sense. The effort required to produce a piece of work was broadly similar across researchers. The number of venues was limited, and those venues were themselves ranked. Funding was unequal, but nowhere near as unequal as it is today. And nobody had an LLM to help draft the manuscript.

    Under those conditions, the number of works someone had and the citations those works received were a reasonable indication of quality. Today the count tells us very little, because almost anything can be published somewhere. Even this blog post could be published if I wanted it to be (I don't). And I am talking about peer-reviewed venues, with the work published as peer-reviewed research. Citations still carry some signal, and various normalisations can make comparisons fairer across fields, for instance by accounting for how many venues exist and therefore how many citations are realistically available. From there, it is a short step to aggregating numbers by department or institution. But the foundation underneath all of it has weakened. Every condition I described above has changed, and the effects compound. Some of the new venues will publish almost anything for a fee. And with so many more papers in circulation, citations have inflated too, helped along by self-citation, citation circles and reviewers who ask authors to cite their own work. The numbers keep going up, and they mean less every year.

    How did we get here? The machinery of measurement has a long history. In 1955, Eugene Garfield proposed a citation index for science, the idea that would later give us the journal impact factor. In 1963, Derek de Solla Price published Little Science, Big Science, which helped inspire a new field devoted to measuring science itself. By the end of the decade it had a name, scientometrics, and in 1978 it had its own journal. Science had started counting itself, and it has not stopped since. What began as a way of understanding science gradually became a way of judging scientists.

    Ranking researchers came next. The h-index, proposed by Jorge Hirsch in 2005, is defined as the largest number h such that you have h papers each cited at least h times. The intention was good. Its appeal was that it rewarded consistency instead of a single lucky hit. Its weakness is that it never penalises papers with few citations, so in a world where publications proliferate, publishing more simply raises your chances of a higher score. The corrections followed quickly: the g-index, the A-index, the R-index, the e-index, the hg-index, the h(2)-index, and more. The length of that list says something by itself. When a measure needs that many repairs, perhaps the problem lies in what we are asking it to do. And the variants created a new problem of their own. With so many ways of ranking a researcher, there is always one that makes you look good, built on criteria you happen to like. What started as a well-meant attempt to measure quality has slowly got out of control.

    Soon it was the turn of institutions. Universities, institutes and departments began to be ranked, partly on the strength of their researchers and partly on their other activities. The Academic Ranking of World Universities appeared in 2003, followed by Times Higher Education and QS. ARWU claims to be objective because it relies only on quantitative indicators, although its choice of indicators and weights is itself a judgement. The others openly include reputation surveys and other subjective components. Universities began using rankings to attract students, to strengthen grant applications, to negotiate influence. Ranking became a business, and a profitable one. The companies that produce the major rankings also sell universities consultancy, data analysis, benchmarking and advertising. In other words, the same organisations that judge universities also sell them advice on how to be judged more favourably. The companies say their rankings are kept separate from their commercial services, but at least one study has found that universities buying services from a ranker climbed that ranker's table faster than expected. Whatever the truth in each case, a system in which the judge also sells services to the judged deserves more scrutiny than it gets. Universities now live and die by the rankings they helped to popularise, and pay for the privilege.

    Every ranking is a simplification. It takes the enormous variety of what researchers and universities do, the teaching, the mentoring, the slow and uncertain work of discovery, the service to communities, and compresses it into a single position on a list. Some simplification is unavoidable, and I am not against measurement as such. My concern is what happens when the simplification becomes the target. The economist Charles Goodhart first described the problem in 1975, and the anthropologist Marilyn Strathern later put it in the form most of us know, in a paper about audit in British universities: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. She wrote that in 1997. We have had almost thirty years to listen. People start working towards the ranking and away from what the research should be. It is a deeply flawed system, and we are all dragged into it whether we like it or not.

    When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

    We need to review these practices collectively, because they are damaging the very process of education and research they claim to describe. Some of this has already begun, through initiatives such as DORA and CoARA, but signing a declaration is easier than changing how a hiring committee actually decides. Universities, funders and researchers all have a part to play: in how we hire and promote, in how we assess grant applications, in which numbers we choose to quote about ourselves. We need systems that cannot simply be optimised for or lobbied for, so that a good position on a list can only be earned by doing the work well.

    There is another layer to this system, and it is the one that costs us most directly. Authors are increasingly required to pay article processing charges to publish their work, and those charges are becoming prohibitive. Some of the most prestigious venues now charge over £9,000, close to £10,000, for a single paper. That money usually comes from grants and university budgets, which means, in most cases, from public funds. And the cost does not fall equally. Researchers in less wealthy countries, at smaller institutions, in less well-funded fields, or at the start of their careers are the ones most likely to be priced out of the venues that count most. A system that claims to reward excellence ends up rewarding access to money, and deepening the very disparities that so much of our research sets out to document. Some of these same venues publish important work on inequality in science, while their charges quietly contribute to it. What justifies this? Why do we accept it?

    We are hostages of a ranking system we created ourselves.

    We accept it because we are hostages of a ranking system we created ourselves. Publishing in the most prestigious venues counts towards our h-index, our promotions, our grant applications and our university's position on a list, so we pay whatever is asked. And what do we get for that money? The submission process, for a start, remains as cumbersome as ever. Authors are still responsible for formatting requirements that have nothing to do with the science, for navigating systems that seem designed for a previous decade, and for waiting months for a decision. If I am expected to pay close to £10,000 on acceptance, surely it would be fair for some of that money to reward the reviewers, who still do this work as volunteers. But I digress.

    Then there is the quality of the review itself. Reviewers can be wrong. I have received many reviews that were simply wrong, and authors are still required to answer them point by point, as though every comment carried equal weight. Having served as an editor myself, I know how hard it is to find reviewers at all, and I wrote about that experience in an earlier post. But knowing the difficulty does not make the errors acceptable. When authors appeal, editors often seem reluctant to admit that a reviewer may have made a mistake. They hesitate. The process has very little room for the possibility that the person judging the work misunderstood it.

    All of this brings me back to rankings. Young researchers today have everything on the line. They compete for a shrinking number of positions, against established researchers with large groups and resources, and now against LLMs that can help produce papers at a pace no individual can match. They pay to publish, they wait months for reviews that may be wrong, and they are judged by numbers that reward volume more than substance.

    We have to think about a new model, one in which quality is what gets rewarded, ahead of the profits of publishers and the interests of ranking agencies. These companies can exist. They can even be useful. What they should not do is dictate what counts as good science, or decide who can afford to take part in it. Academia created this machinery to evaluate itself, which means it is also within our power to change it.

    So, are you a scientist? Then the next time you are asked for your h-index, your citation count or your university's position on a list, give it if you must. But talk first about what you discovered, who you taught, and what you helped someone else to understand. I should confess that I am part of this too. My own website lists my h-index, and I will probably keep it there. People can list whatever they like about themselves. What matters is that we read these numbers with a pinch of salt, or perhaps a whole cellar of it, and that we slowly stop giving them the weight they have today. For my part, I will try never to ask for them when I am the one assessing a candidate, a proposal or a colleague. That is what we built academia for: to educate people and to generate knowledge. Everything else should follow from it.
